Thank you for submitting the revised version of your article "Temporal cascade of frontal, motor and muscle processes underlying human action-stopping" for consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers. The reviewers have discussed the reviews. The evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor (Wery van den Wildenberg) and Richard Ivry as the Senior Editor. The Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

The thorough review reports of the previous review round match the vast nature and the wide scope of the original manuscript. The resulting rebuttal letter that accompanied the revision also reflects a broad discussion, which is commendable. Concerning the revised manuscript, there are a few issues left to be discussed.

These issues are addressed in detail at the end of this letter. Here I provide a brief summary:

The first remaining issue concerns the request to not merely acknowledge connecting studies by citing them, but to also address and integrate the findings of these relevant studies vis-a-vis the current work. In this respect, the rebuttal letter provides a more balanced account, and that tone might be extended to the manuscript.

The second issue concerns the timing when stopping reaches the muscle in relation to the model. This point has been brought to your attention by the Senior Editor, a few days before this decision letter, to facilitate the exchange process. Below you can find the whole line of reasoning (main point 2). More data, additional analyses or simulation studies are not required (or even asked) at this point. A discussion of the seemingly controversial time-courses would be sufficient.

Elaboration on these issues:

1) The authors wrote a detailed and insightful response, which essentially clarified my methodological questions. Some of the more conceptual issues were answered well in the response letter, yet the changes in the manuscript were less substantial than what one might have expected.

a) E.g., regarding Wessel's beta-burst analysis: the authors now cite this work (Results), but rather casually so. The manuscript does not try to compare or integrate the presented findings with Wessel's.

b) The same goes for the partial EMG work. Most of the studies we provided in the first round of the review are cited, but again rather offhand. The manuscript does not really integrate the different studies. Several studies already used an estimate essentially the same to what the authors still refer to as "our idea of CancelTime" (although admittedly these claims have been toned down), yet no attempt is made to compare these estimates, their correlations with SSRTs etc.

c) In some ways, I find that some of the claims made are not founded well enough in data, and the authors seem to be aware of it: "we agree that the temporal cascade model that we have constructed is only approximate as it is averaged across participants who had different stopping latencies, and is also contingent on, as the reviewers' rightly point out, on statistical procedures."

Yet again, the manuscript has not really been changed in accordance with this. Still, it is not properly discussed, for example, that the exact timing estimates heavily rely on the choice of latency estimates (EMG/MEP onsets or peak, of which each again can be calculated in many different ways.

2) I reviewed the initial submission of this manuscript. The manuscript is significantly improved in many ways. The editor requested that we evaluate whether claims have been toned down, previous work on EMG and beta-bursts have been acknowledged, and main point 6 regarding the timing estimate of CancelTime and a ballistic phase have been addressed. I think the first two points have been sufficiently addressed. However, the authors response to Main Point 6, especially their point 3, has raised new concerns about their claims about timing of stopping.

The authors present a 3-part response to main point 6. Part 1 points out that SSRTemg is similar to CancelTime and argues that this is consistent with the remaining ~60ms difference between CancelTime and SSRTbeh being a ballistic stage. Part 2 presents simulations consistent with a ballistic stage that is 34-47ms long (which is perhaps less than the ~60ms difference between canceltime and SSRTbeh). Point 3 argues that the real end of the race (at least as a criterion for evaluating CancelTime) is when EMG amplitude exceeds the threshold set on PartialEMG trials. They show that on correct go trials this threshold is exceeded ~100ms after the average stop signal would occur. Given the SSD tracking algorithm that ensured that the race between going and stopping is roughly tied, then the real latency of the stop process (as measured by EMG) may be ~100ms, so CancelTime may actually be an overestimate of the average stop latency.

The part 3 simulation results seem to conflict with multiple pieces of evidence in the manuscript and the literature. It appears that the authors are suggesting that the ballistic stage may be ~120ms (~220ms SSRTbeh minus the ~100ms stop process), which is both inconsistent with the simulation results in part 2 and inconsistent with the previous literature presented in the manuscript (e.g., Gopal and Muphy, 2016; Jana and Murthy, 2018 suggested 50ms for reaching movements). It also seems to bring into question the entire temporal sequence presented in the manuscript. Why would the end of the race be observable in muscles at 100ms if the signal to stop from cortex (perhaps rIFG) occurs 20ms later at 120ms?

Additionally, none of the 3 parts of the response have directly addressed the reviewers' main point 6. To briefly reiterate, assuming a race model, the ~50% of trials that are true failed stops (an overt response occurs) should tend to have the longest SSDs, fastest go RTs, and slowest SSRTs. The ~25% of trials that are successful stops with no EMG should be the opposite: shortest SSDs, slowest go RTs, and fastest SSRTs. This leaves the ~25% of trials that are successful stops with EMG, which should be in between these extremes. However, because there are ~twice as many stop failures as stop successes, the partial EMG trials will tend have shorter SSDs, slower go RT, and faster SSRTs than each measure's overall average. Therefore, CancelTime may be an underestimate of the true central tendency of SSRT across all stop trials.

In the text, the authors seem to agree with parts of this point, at least in part. They say "CancelTime… does not include the stopping latencies of the No EMG trials, which presumably reflect the fastest stopping latencies where the Stop process was fast enough to cancel the impending response before it reaches the muscle". However, they do not point out that CancelTime also does not include stop-failure trials, which presumably reflect the slowest stopping latencies, leaving CancelTime to reflect stopping latencies that are faster than the slowest half of stop trials but slower than the fastest quarter of stop trials. Also, in Figures 1G-I in their response, they illustrate how they believe correct stops with No EMG, correct stops with partial EMG, and failed stops arise from an accumulator model framework. No EMG has the fastest stop process, failed stop has the slowest stop process, and partial EMG is in between.

To conclude, I do not think that the response to main point 6 addressed the original concern, and I believe that the new simulations bring up new questions about the temporal cascade of processes in stopping. Does the stop process reach the muscle ~150-160ms after the stop signal, as suggested by CancelTime and SSRTemg, or is it ~100ms after the stop signal, as seemingly suggested by their part 3 in response to Main Point 6? If the latter, then how does this fit in with TMS evidence of motor suppression at ~140ms or beta-burst in cortex (perhaps rIFG) at 120ms? Also, if the argument from Main Point 6 is valid (and the authors do not address its validity directly), how can this be synthesized with the Part 3 response suggesting that CancelTime is an overestimate of the latency of the stop process?

results.result: Studies 1 and 2 demonstrate that partial EMG responses occur on approximately 50% of successful stop trials, with amplitudes ~50% smaller than full keypresses. CancelTime (the time when EMG activity begins to decline after the stop signal) was measured at ~147 ms across both studies, which is approximately 60 ms shorter than the behavioral SSRT (~207 ms). CancelTime was positively correlated with SSRTBeh in both studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C25 provide converging evidence from two independent samples showing consistent patterns of partial EMG responses and their timing. The statistical analyses are appropriate with adequate sample sizes (n=10 and n=32), significant correlations (r=0.71 and r=0.59), and strong Bayes factors. The replication across studies strengthens the findings.

results.result: The ~60 ms difference between CancelTime and SSRTBeh is attributed to a ballistic stage in movement execution. When SSRT was recalculated using EMG responses (SSRTEMG = 157±7 ms) instead of behavioral responses, it was significantly faster than SSRTBeh (207±3 ms) but not significantly different from CancelTime. The EMG profile on partial trials diverged from full response trials ~55 ms after EMG onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C31, C53-C54 are well-supported by the data showing SSRTEMG matches CancelTime better than SSRTBeh (C29-C30), with appropriate statistical tests and large effect sizes (d=1.3, BF10>100). The ballistic stage hypothesis is supported by citations to prior work (C27-C28) and the EMG profile analysis (C31). However, the exact duration and mechanism of the ballistic stage remain somewhat inferential.

results.result: CancelTime was validated as a measure of stopping latency through correlations with BEESTS model estimates. Mean CancelTime correlated with mean SSRTBEESTS (r=0.54), the variability (SD) of CancelTime correlated with SD of SSRTBEESTS (r=0.42), and trigger failure percentage correlated with mean CancelTime (ρ=0.57).
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35, C49 demonstrate convergent validity through multiple correlations with an established computational model (BEESTS). All correlations are statistically significant with moderate to strong effect sizes and strong Bayes factors (BF10>6.9). The consistency across different model parameters (mean, SD, trigger failures) strengthens the interpretation that CancelTime reflects stopping implementation.

results.result: Study 3 using TMS demonstrated that global motor suppression begins at ~140 ms after the stop signal, approximately 20 ms before the mean CancelTime of ~160 ms. MEP amplitudes in a task-irrelevant muscle (ECR) were significantly suppressed at 140 ms and 180 ms after the stop signal. The corticospinal conduction time was measured at 23±0.3 ms, accounting for the delay between cortical suppression and muscle-level effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39, C51, C61, C79 are well-supported by TMS data with appropriate statistical analyses (n=17, significant t-tests with large effect sizes and BF10>39.8). The timing relationship between global motor suppression (~140 ms) and CancelTime (~160 ms) is consistent with the measured corticospinal conduction time (~23 ms), providing physiological plausibility. The trial-by-trial analysis (C39) further validates the temporal relationship.

results.result: Studies 4 and 5 using EEG demonstrated that right frontal beta burst percentage increased for successful stop trials compared to baseline and correct go trials. Mean BurstTime (~115-129 ms) was significantly shorter than CancelTime (~166-169 ms) in both studies. Across participants, there was a strong positive correlation between BurstTime and CancelTime in both studies individually (Study 4: ρ=0.76; Study 5: ρ=0.57) and when pooled (ρ=0.66).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C48, C56-C57 are supported by converging evidence from two independent EEG studies with appropriate statistical analyses. The replication of the BurstTime-CancelTime correlation across studies strengthens the finding. However, the authors acknowledge limitations including low burst percentage (~15%, C68) and no difference in CancelTime between trials with and without bursts (C69), which somewhat weakens the interpretation of necessity/sufficiency.

results.result: The manuscript proposes a temporal cascade model of action-stopping: right frontal beta activity increases at ~120 ms (likely reflecting rIFC/preSMA activation), followed by global motor suppression at ~140 ms (reflecting basal ganglia output via STN and GPi), then muscle-level suppression at ~160 ms (CancelTime), and finally behavioral stopping at ~220 ms (SSRTBeh). This implies neural events mediating stopping must occur before ~140 ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C55, C58-C60, C62-C63, C80 synthesize findings across all five studies into a coherent temporal model. Each timing estimate is supported by direct empirical data from the respective studies. The model is physiologically plausible given known anatomy and conduction times. However, the model involves some inference about neural pathways (C59-C60) based on prior literature rather than direct measurement in this study.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence support the interpretation that partial EMG activity represents an actively suppressed response rather than merely weak Go activation: (1) correlation with SSRTBeh, (2) correlation with BEESTS model estimates, (3) similar initial EMG profile to full responses that diverges ~55 ms after onset, (4) coincidence with TMS-measured global motor suppression, and (5) amplitude increases with SSD.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C52 represent interpretive conclusions supported by multiple converging lines of evidence presented throughout the manuscript. The evidence is strong and multifaceted, using different methodologies (EMG, TMS, computational modeling) that all point to the same interpretation. The alternative hypothesis (weak Go activation) is explicitly addressed and ruled out based on the EMG profile analysis and SSD-amplitude relationship.

results.result: CancelTime likely overestimates the brain's true stopping latency because it does not account for corticospinal conduction time (~20-23 ms, though this may underestimate the true mean conduction time) and does not include No EMG trials where stopping occurred before any muscle activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65, C77-C78 are logical inferences based on the measured corticospinal conduction time and the existence of No EMG trials. The acknowledgment that TMS-evoked MEP onset latency underestimates true conduction time (C64-C65) is appropriately cautious and supported by citations. The inference about No EMG trials (C78) is reasonable but somewhat speculative as these trials were not directly analyzed.

results.result: MEPs were also suppressed in Failed Stop trials compared to Correct Go trials, but with a delay relative to Successful Stop trials and CancelTime, suggesting the Stop process is initiated even in Failed Stop trials but implemented later.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by the trial-by-trial TMS analysis shown in Figure 4d. The interpretation that delayed Stop process implementation contributes to stopping failure is reasonable and consistent with race model frameworks. However, the authors appropriately note an alternative explanation (faster Go process completion).

results.result: The burst percentage on Successful Stop trials was relatively low (~15%), and CancelTimes did not differ between trials with and without detected bursts in Study 5. The authors speculate this could be due to poor EEG signal-to-noise or that bursts on Go trials might reflect proactive slowing.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 report empirical findings that somewhat complicate the interpretation of beta bursts' role in stopping. The low burst percentage and lack of CancelTime difference between burst/no-burst trials (C69) raise questions about necessity/sufficiency. The explanations offered (C70-C71) are speculative and not directly tested. This represents an important limitation that the authors appropriately acknowledge.

results.result: The current study found right frontal beta bursts, whereas Wessel (2020) found dorsomedial frontal bursts. This discrepancy may be due to methodological differences (spatial filter vs. channel space analysis). Both studies observed motor cortex suppression ~20-25 ms after frontal bursts.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 appropriately contextualize the current findings relative to prior work. The methodological explanation for the discrepancy (C73) is plausible though speculative. The convergence on timing of motor suppression following frontal activity (C75) strengthens confidence in the temporal cascade despite spatial localization differences.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that timings in their model are approximations dependent on various factors (averaging, different experiments, detection algorithms), but note striking convergence with timings reported in other studies for CancelTime, MEP suppression, conduction time, BurstTime, and ballistic stage duration.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 represent appropriate scientific caution (C82) balanced with confidence based on convergence across studies (C83). The citations to multiple independent studies reporting similar timings (C83) strengthen the generalizability of the findings. This represents good scientific practice in acknowledging limitations while contextualizing findings.

results.result: The current results are compatible with the interactive race model (Stop process begins late but implementation is quick) and the BEESTS model (trigger process duration ~80-120 ms).
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 appropriately relate the empirical findings to existing computational models. The compatibility with the interactive race model is supported by the observation of late but rapid stopping implementation. The BEESTS compatibility is supported by the timing of beta bursts (~120 ms) preceding motor suppression. These are reasonable interpretations though not definitive tests of the models.

results.result: The authors predict that CancelTime and beta burst time will be more sensitive than SSRTBeh for discriminating patients from controls and will show stronger correlations with self-reported impulsivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 are predictions about future work rather than results from the current studies. While these predictions are reasonable based on the current findings showing CancelTime is less contaminated by peripheral delays, they remain untested hypotheses. No clinical or self-report data are presented in the current manuscript.

results.result: The manuscript reviews established knowledge about response inhibition, SSRT, and prior findings suggesting SSRT may overestimate brain stopping latency. Previous studies showed EMG decline at ~150 ms, MEP reduction at ~150 ms, global MEP suppression at ~150 ms linked to subthalamic nucleus, and increased right frontal beta power during stopping.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C14 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These provide essential context and motivation for the current studies. The citations appear accurate and relevant. This represents appropriate scholarly contextualization of the research question.

results.result: The authors suggest that maximum CancelTime reflects the last point at which stopping can prevent responses, and that CancelTime narrows the time window for causal manipulation of neural structures involved in stopping.
results.evaluation: Claims C76, C81 are reasonable inferences based on the ballistic stage hypothesis and the timing data. The interpretation that CancelTime represents a critical temporal boundary is logical given the evidence. The implication for experimental design (C81) is a valid practical consequence of the findings.
